hints: Start by thinking about the main practical problem - only a tiny fraction of bacteria actually take up a plasmid during transformation, so how would you pick them out?
Remember what is built into the vector - a marker gene is added to the plasmid alongside the gene of interest so both are transferred together.
Think about what a fluorescent protein does when you shine a particular type of light on the culture plate.
Think about the other type of marker - an enzyme that converts a colourless substrate into a coloured or easily stained product.
Consider what happens if the gene of interest is inserted into or very close to the marker gene and disrupts it - what does loss of signal tell you?
Extend the idea beyond bacteria to whole plants or animals, and recall named examples and why these markers are safe to use.
walkthrough:
Why a visible marker is needed**
Transformation is very inefficient. Most bacteria on the plate have not taken up the plasmid, and they all look identical. Linking a gene that produces an easily seen product to your gene of interest means any cell that glows or changes colour must have taken up the DNA.

How the two types of marker work**
GFP codes for green fluorescent protein which emits bright green light when exposed to UV light. Other markers code for enzymes such as beta-galactosidase or GUS which act on a substrate to produce a visible colour change or easily stained substance. In both cases you get a simple visual screen without killing the cells.

Finding transformants and recombinants**
Put the marker gene on the plasmid vector. Transformed bacteria show the marker signal, non-transformed do not, so transformed colonies are easy to pick out. If you clone the gene of interest into or close to the marker gene, you disrupt the marker. A colony that has the plasmid but has lost the colour or fluorescence must contain recombinant DNA. The same principle lets you spot transgenic plants or animals that express the marker.

Final answer: Marker gene added to vector/plasmid with gene of interest. Fluorescent marker e.g. GFP emits bright light when exposed to UV light. Enzyme marker e.g. beta-galactosidase / GUS gives visible colour change when stained. Allows easy identification of transformed bacteria and of transgenic organisms. If gene of interest inserted into / close to marker gene, disruption identifies recombinant DNA/plasmid. Markers pose no known risk.

hints: Start from the global need - how could adding a useful gene increase total food production or crop yield?
Think beyond amount to quality - what traits affecting taste, nutritional value or how long food keeps could be engineered?
Recall a famous rice variety engineered to make a vitamin precursor to prevent deficiency - what nutrient was added?
Think about abiotic stress - how could tolerance to drought, heat, salt or poor soils help farming?
Think about biotic stress - how would genes for insect or fungal disease resistance help the crop grow?
Think about competition with weeds - what is the advantage if the crop alone can survive a herbicide spray?
Link reduced spraying to two groups - what is the cost and health benefit to the farmer and the benefit to food chains and pollinators?
Consider fertiliser use - what if cereals could be given the nitrogen-fixing ability of legumes?
Remember to anchor your discussion with specific named examples linking the crop to the exact improvement.
walkthrough:
More and better food**
Adding genes for faster growth or larger seeds increases yields and helps food security. Other genes improve quality, taste and keeping properties. The classic Flavr Savr tomato stays firm in storage so it can ripen on the vine for better flavour.

Healthier and tougher crops**
Genes for vitamin or mineral synthesis improve human nutrition. Golden Rice makes extra beta-carotene for vitamin A to prevent blindness and deficiency. Genes for drought, heat, salt or disease tolerance let crops grow with climate change and on poor quality land with less fertiliser.

Pest, weed and environmental benefits**
Bt maize and Bt cotton make Bt insecticidal protein that kills leaf-eating insects, giving pest, insect and fungal disease resistance. Herbicide-resistant crops survive spraying while weeds are killed, reducing competition. Both traits mean less pesticide use, which is cost effective and healthier for the farmer and leaves less damage to food chains and pollinators. In future, engineering nitrogen-fixing ability into non-leguminous cereals would further cut fertiliser need.

Final answer: Advantages include: increased food production / crop yields; improved quality, taste and keeping properties e.g. Flavr Savr tomato stores better and can ripen on vine; added nutrients e.g. Golden Rice with extra vitamin A; tolerance to climate change and ability to grow on poor land with less fertiliser; pest / insect / fungal resistance e.g. Bt maize / Bt cotton killing leaf-eating insects, so less pesticide needed; herbicide resistance reducing weed competition; potential nitrogen-fixation in non-legumes; benefits to farmer in cost and health and to environment via less impact on food chains and pollinators.
